more.title: 'Mega heat waves' strengthened by interaction between soil moisture, atmospheric pressure and temperature
more.summary: A new study has found that a self-reinforcing interaction between temperature, soil moisture and atmospheric pressure is being triggered at high temperatures, making extreme heat waves 10% hotter than they would otherwise be. The study was published in Science Advances and led by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA).

more.title: Redefining honesty in a crisis: Why truth alone is not enough
more.summary: When a company suffers a cyberattack, leaks customer data or faces a major public scandal, telling the truth is essential. But new research suggests it is not enough on its own: organizations also need to communicate early, treat people with respect and show how they intend to put things right.

more.title: Atom-scale model could help improve material growth for advanced electronics
more.summary: Penn State researchers have refined an atom-scale model of how silicon carbide changes from a solid into vapor during crystal growth, work that could help manufacturers produce higher-quality material for advanced electronics while reducing costly trial-and-error experiments.

more.title: Scientists achieve record-breaking low temperature on China's space station, paving the way for new physics experiments
more.summary: Matter starts to behave differently at extremely low temperatures, creating conditions ideal for studying quantum physics and new states of matter. Now, researchers from China have achieved a new low-temperature record aboard their Tiangong space station. Their research, recently published in Science, might lead to a new generation of experiments in quantum physics and precision measurements in space.

more.title: MTG-I2 satellite delivers remarkable first images, capturing a weather view of Europe every 2.5 minutes
more.summary: Europe's meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT, has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite's launch on Aug. 27, 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes.

more.title: Disasters and debt. Escaping the 'climate-debt doom loop'
more.summary: It took around 480,000 trucks to haul away 4.8 million metric tons (5.3 million tons) of rubble across western Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa tore through the Caribbean in 2025, United Nations satellites showed.

more.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
more.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

more.title: Untangling the patterns of the cosmic microwave background to better understand the early universe
more.summary: A figure in red trudges across a blanket of white. Snow squeaks under the scientist's feet, too dry to be slick or soft. Only a line of flags and a few large buildings—the scientist's destination—break up the landscape. The sun hovers on the horizon, never quite setting against a blue sky devoid of clouds.

more.title: The wins and weak spots in America's solar supply chain
more.author: Julian Spector
more.summary: See more from Canary Media’s ​“Chart of the Week” column . Now that solar has become America’s go-to choice for new power plants , the pressure is on to assemble a fully domestic supply chain for the technology. Data from the latest Clean Investment Monitor shows that this onshoring process is well underway.…

more.title: Spot a baby bird on the ground? Don't be tempted to bird‑nap it
more.summary: Spring is the season of blooming flowers and buzzing bees.

more.title: The wasps that horrified Darwin reveal evolution's one-way streets
more.summary: Few insects have a more gruesome lifestyle than Darwin wasps. Rather than simply hunting other animals, these parasitic wasps lay their eggs on or inside living hosts, including caterpillars, beetles and spiders. Their larvae then feed on their hosts, gradually consuming them and eventually killing them.

more.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
more.summary: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make…

more.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
more.summary: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism.

more.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
more.summary: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

more.title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
more.author: Jacek Krywko
more.summary: Explaining the Great Unconformity, where Cambrian deposits sit on top of older rocks.

more.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
more.summary: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

more.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
more.summary: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible.

more.title: European forests need to solve two crises—but not necessarily in one place
more.summary: Forest areas can act both as carbon sinks and as vital habitats for thousands of species—but not necessarily at the same time. This has important implications for how Europe should manage its forests, says a University of Copenhagen researcher.

more.title: High-precision timeline helps clarify an ancient magma surge in the North Cascades
more.summary: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal. However, what triggers these extreme surges, which last tens of millions of years, can be unclear.

more.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: AI, Defense And Space Tech Lead For Large Rounds
more.author: Joanna Glasner
more.summary: This week brought another plethora of large funding rounds for startups and growth-stage companies. Shield AI, a defense tech player focused on autonomy and virtual simulations, secured the largest financing, bringing in $2 billion. Next on the list was drone delivery provider Zipline International, which pulled in a fresh $1.5 billion.

more.title: AI won't ever make a historically accurate film—but it could help archaeology create better stories
more.summary: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer's "Odyssey" by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticized for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story "historically accurate and true to the art of Homer" at a fraction of the cost, he…

more.title: Smart packaging film 'lights up' under UV as meat loses freshness
more.summary: Food spoilage causes chemical changes that are not always easy to detect by appearance alone. To provide a clearer indication of freshness and quality, researchers at Kyushu University have developed a smart packaging film that changes color and glows under ultraviolet (UV) light as meat loses freshness.

more.title: The worse climate change gets, the harder it becomes to stop it
more.summary: This year may be seen as a turning point in the climate crisis. The U.N. has accepted that global warming is going to exceed 1.5°C, while climate scientists have concluded that the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade.

more.title: Noise pollution changes biology or behavior in 80% of animal species studied
more.summary: We live in a noisy world. Whether it is the roar of traffic, the rumble of ships or the hum of heavy industry, there is often no escaping noise unless you are a hermit on a desert island.
